title: The Red Badge of Courage
author: Stephen Crane
setting: An unnamed Civil War battlefield in Virginia, over roughly two days
lengthNote: Twenty-four short chapters covering about forty-eight hours
openingLine: The cold passed reluctantly from the earth, and the retiring fogs revealed an army stretched out on the hills, resting.
summary: A farm boy enlists expecting Greek battles and finds a muddy camp full of rumour. When the fighting comes he holds, then runs, then wanders among the wounded until another fleeing soldier cracks his skull with a rifle butt — an injury his regiment reads as evidence of courage. Crane, who was born six years after the war ended and had never seen a battle, wrote the whole thing from inside one frightened private's head and never names the battle, the cause or, for most of the book, the private.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Red Badge of Courage
sourceText.note: This is the 1895 Appleton book text, which is shorter than Crane's surviving manuscript. Editions based on the manuscript restore a good deal of Henry's self-justifying reasoning and change the balance of the ending.

atAGlance.label: Serial
atAGlance.note: A shortened version went out through newspaper syndication before any publisher would take the book.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: D. Appleton and Company, New York. Crane was twenty-three and instantly famous.

atAGlance.label: The battle
atAGlance.note: The circumstances have long been associated with Chancellorsville in May 1863, but no place, date or commander is given in the text.

atAGlance.label: Names
atAGlance.value: The youth, the tall soldier, the loud soldier
atAGlance.note: Crane withholds most personal names for chapters at a time, and the epithets are how the army sees its own men.

structure.label: Chapters I–III
structure.title: Rumour, and a private question
structure.summary: The regiment has been camped for months and lives on contradictory reports of a coming move. Henry Fleming, who enlisted against his mother's advice and expecting something Homeric, discovers that the only question that interests him is whether he will run, and that he cannot answer it by reasoning or by watching other men.

scenes.title: The tall soldier's rumour
scenes.summary: A washed shirt brings news of a march; Henry remembers enlisting, and his mother peeling potatoes instead of making a speech.

scenes.title: Comparisons
scenes.summary: He tries to find another man as frightened as he is, and concludes that he is alone in it.

scenes.title: The march
scenes.summary: Knapsacks are thrown away along the road, and Henry realises the regiment cannot be left.

structure.label: Chapters IV–VI
structure.title: He holds, and then he runs
structure.summary: The first assault comes and Henry fires with everybody else, absorbed into the line and briefly free of himself. When a second wave arrives and men on either side begin to go, he goes too — fast, before any argument has taken place in him — and looks back to find that the regiment held.

scenes.title: The line holds
scenes.summary: Henry loses his separate self in the regiment and discovers that courage can be produced by a crowd.

scenes.title: The second charge
scenes.summary: He runs like an insane sprinter, and learns from an officer's shouting that the position was not lost.

structure.label: Chapters VII–XII
structure.title: The forest, the wounded column, the blow
structure.summary: Alone in the woods, Henry builds a case for his own wisdom out of a squirrel and a quiet glade, and then walks into a chapel of pine boughs containing a corpse. He joins a column of wounded men, watches Jim Conklin die, abandons the tattered soldier, and is finally struck on the head by a panicking man from another regiment.

scenes.title: Nature's evidence
scenes.summary: A squirrel runs from a thrown pine cone, which Henry takes as a law; the dead man in the chapel is the reply.

scenes.title: Jim Conklin
scenes.summary: The procession of the wounded, the tattered man's questions, and the tall soldier's death in a field.

scenes.title: The wound
scenes.summary: Henry deserts the tattered soldier, hopes privately for a defeat that would vindicate him, and is clubbed with a rifle in the retreat.

structure.label: Chapters XIII–XVIII
structure.title: Read as a hero
structure.summary: A cheerful stranger walks him back to his own fires, where the regiment assumes his head wound is a graze from a bullet and Wilson nurses him. Henry keeps the account, discovers that the loud soldier has quietly become a serious man, and recovers his swagger in time to overhear a general describe the regiment as mule drivers.

scenes.title: The bandage
scenes.summary: Wilson binds his head and gives up his blanket; nobody asks how the wound was made.

scenes.title: The packet of letters
scenes.summary: Henry holds Wilson's envelope of last words over him, and then fights like a wild man while the regiment watches.

scenes.title: Mule drivers
scenes.summary: Two officers discuss the regiment as an expendable unit within earshot of two of its men.

structure.label: Chapters XIX–XXIV
structure.title: The flag, and the story he settles on
structure.summary: Henry takes the colours from a dying sergeant and carries them through two charges, is called a war devil by men who watched him, and hears the same officer who insulted the regiment praise him by name. In the last chapter he assembles all of it, including the tattered soldier, into an account of himself he can live with.

scenes.title: The colours
scenes.summary: He seizes the flag, the charge falls short, and the regiment is jeered and then defended.

scenes.title: The fence
scenes.summary: A stand under fire, a captured flag, and four prisoners.

scenes.title: The account
scenes.summary: Marching away in the rain, Henry reviews his deeds, flinches at the memory of the tattered man, and decides he is a man.

characters.name: Henry Fleming
characters.role: A private in the 304th New York, called 'the youth' for most of the book
characters.summary: He enlisted for a war he had read about and finds one made of smoke, rumour and other men's faces. Everything that happens to him happens twice: once as an event and again, shortly afterwards, as a version of the event in which he comes off better, and Crane keeps both on the page.
characters.clue: He ran from his first real fight, was knocked senseless by a man from his own side, and let his regiment believe a bullet had done it.
traits: eventually brave, on terms he chooses

relationships.label: friend, rival and keeper of a secret

characters.name: Jim Conklin
characters.summary: He starts the novel by carrying a rumour through the camp on the strength of a washed shirt, and he ends it in a field, refusing help and looking for a place to fall down. Crane gives him the one death in the book described in full, and no consoling language whatever.
characters.clue: He brought the camp its first news of the march, and later walked away from the column to die standing, shaking off every hand that reached for him.

characters.name: Wilson
characters.summary: He begins by announcing his own courage and handing Henry a packet of letters for his family, and comes back from the first day quiet, useful and no longer interested in being watched. He is the novel's evidence that a man can change without narrating the change to himself.
characters.clue: He gave away a packet of last letters before the first battle, survived, and had to ask for it back from a man who had been enjoying the power of holding it.

relationships.label: nurses, and is held to ransom by

characters.name: The tattered soldier
characters.role: A wounded man in the column
characters.summary: He is friendly, badly hurt, losing his grip, and he keeps asking Henry the one question Henry cannot answer: where are you hit. Henry leaves him wandering in a field, and the memory is the only thing in the last chapter that the new self-account cannot absorb.
characters.clue: Shot twice and admiring everyone, he asked a stranger a brotherly question about his wound and was walked away from and left in a field.

characters.name: Henry's mother
characters.role: A farm widow in New York State
characters.summary: She refuses to give her son the send-off he has imagined, keeps peeling potatoes while he announces his enlistment, and tells him to watch out and to remember that he is nothing special in an army of thousands. Her advice is the most accurate assessment of his situation in the novel.
characters.clue: She would not make a speech about her son's country; she gave him socks, blackberry jam and the information that he was one man among many.

characters.name: Lieutenant Hasbrouck
characters.summary: He swears at his men, drags them forward by the collar, and is the first person to see Henry fight. He is also the one who passes Henry's name upward, which is how a private's private crisis becomes a matter of official record.
characters.clue: He cursed his company along like a fishwife and then told a colonel the names of the two men who carried the colours.

characters.name: The 304th New York
characters.role: Henry's regiment, treated throughout as a single creature
characters.summary: Crane describes it as a box, a machine, a worm and a dragon, and gives it moods of its own that run ahead of any individual's decision. It is the thing that makes Henry brave in Chapter V and the thing he cannot escape in Chapter III, and a general disposes of it in a sentence as the unit he can best spare.
characters.clue: It is called a box, a machine and a worm, it can be brave before any man in it has decided to be, and a general sacrifices it because it fights like a lot of mule drivers.

themes.name: What courage is evidence of
themes.summary: Henry wants a fact about himself that can be established once and then relied on, and the novel refuses to supply one. Courage in these chapters is produced by crowds, by rage at an insult, by fear of being seen, and it never becomes a property a man can own between engagements.
themes.development: The unanswerable question of Chapters I–II, the borrowed courage of the first stand, the flight, and the final charges made in a temper about the words 'mule drivers'.

themes.name: The story he tells about himself
themes.summary: Every action Henry takes is followed by a version of it in which he acted rightly, and Crane keeps the narration close enough to make the versions persuasive. The book's real subject is not whether he is brave but how quickly a mind can manufacture the account it needs.
themes.development: The squirrel as proof in Chapter VII, the private hope for a defeat in Chapter XI, the wound accepted as a battle scar, and the settled narrative of Chapter XXIV with the tattered man still in it.

themes.name: Manhood and gender
themes.summary: Henry's fear is not of dying but of being seen to be the kind of man who runs, and the last line of the book awards him the title he has been chasing. The one woman in the novel declines to supply the heroic language he wants, and his mother's flat advice keeps returning to correct the story.
themes.development: The refused send-off in Chapter I, the shame of the unwounded man among the wounded in Chapter IX, the epithet 'war devil' in Chapter XVII, and the three words that close Chapter XXIV.

themes.name: The regiment as a body
themes.summary: Individual nerve counts for less in this novel than the state of the thing a man is standing in. The regiment is described in the vocabulary of animals and machinery, it acquires moods before its members do, and a general can decide to spend it in one line of dialogue overheard by two of its privates.
themes.development: The moving box of Chapter III, the welded common personality of Chapter V, the mule-driver conversation of Chapter XVIII, and the collective rage that carries the last charges.

themes.name: Nature's indifference
themes.summary: Henry keeps asking the landscape for a verdict and it keeps declining to give one. He reads a fleeing squirrel as a law of self-preservation and walks straight into a chapel of trees with a rotting corpse in it, and the sun goes on standing in the sky like a pasted wafer over the death of his friend.
themes.development: The religion of peace in Chapter VII, the dead man among the pines, the red sun over Jim Conklin's body, and the sunlight in the last paragraph that refuses to mean anything in particular.

themes.name: War without an overview
themes.summary: No battle is named, no campaign explained, no cause argued. What the private knows is smoke, noise, shouted contradictions and the men within a few yards of him, and the novel's method is to refuse the reader any information Henry does not have.
themes.development: Rumour in Chapter I, the local and partial fighting of Chapters IV–VI, the wandering of Chapters VII–XII, and the absence at the end of any statement about who won.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that takes on the vocabulary and bias of the character it follows.
techniques.inThisBook: The prose adopts Henry's reasoning without endorsing it, so that his case for running is made in his own inflated terms while the sentences quietly leave room for the reader to decline it.

techniques.name: Colour as feeling
techniques.definition: Colour used to register emotional and physical states rather than to describe appearance.
techniques.inThisBook: Red eyes across the river, the red sickness of battle, the red badge itself, a blue demonstration, a corpse's uniform faded to green: colour arrives before information does, which is how the book keeps the reader at the private's eye level.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Men and formations described as creatures.
techniques.inThisBook: Dragons advance, the army is a worm, war is a red animal and a blood-swollen god, and men develop teeth and claws when cornered — the effect is to remove heroism from the vocabulary altogether.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: The wound that certifies Henry's courage is given to him by a terrified man on his own side, and the regiment's finest hour is arranged by a general who chose it as the unit he could best spare.

techniques.name: Naming by epithet
techniques.definition: Characters identified by a single visible attribute instead of a name.
techniques.inThisBook: The youth, the tall soldier, the loud soldier, the tattered man: the labels are how an army sees its own people, and Crane withholds Henry's name for most of the book so that the reader inherits that view.

techniques.name: Simile
techniques.definition: An explicit comparison, usually brief, doing the work of a longer description.
techniques.inThisBook: The most famous sentence in the book is a five-word comparison — the sun pasted in the sky like a wafer — placed alone as a paragraph immediately after a death, and refusing to say anything more.

quotations.text: The cold passed reluctantly from the earth, and the retiring fogs revealed an army stretched out on the hills, resting.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The two active verbs belong to the weather, and the army is merely revealed by it, lying still. Before a single man has spoken, the grammar has established the arrangement the book will keep: the natural world does things, and the soldiers are things it does them to.

quotations.text: He had grown to regard himself merely as a part of a vast blue demonstration.
quotations.context: After months of drill and no fighting.
quotations.analysis: A war is reduced to a colour and a gesture, as though the Union army were a piece of political theatre he has been hired to stand in. 'Merely' is Henry's word, not Crane's, and it registers the disappointment of a boy who enlisted for something with names in it.

quotations.text: He was a mental outcast.
quotations.context: After failing to find any other man visibly wrestling with the same fear.
quotations.analysis: Four words on their own, and the isolation is entirely self-generated: he has been reading other men's faces and finding nothing, which proves only that they are doing the same thing he is. The novel's first joke is that everyone in the regiment believes himself the only coward in it.

quotations.text: And there were iron laws of tradition and law on four sides. He was in a moving box.
quotations.context: On realising that he cannot simply leave the regiment on the march.
quotations.analysis: The image turns a body of comrades into a container with walls, and the repetition of 'law' inside one clause makes the enclosure sound legal rather than social. It also sets up the chapters ahead: when he does escape the box, he finds that there is nowhere outside it to be.

quotations.text: He suddenly lost concern for himself, and forgot to look at a menacing fate. He became not a man but a member.
quotations.context: During the first assault, firing with the rest of the line.
quotations.analysis: Courage arrives here as a loss rather than an achievement — of self-consciousness, and then of separate selfhood. The pun on 'member' is doing real work: he is briefly a limb of something larger, which is exactly the condition he cannot reproduce when he is alone in Chapter VI.

quotations.text: He felt that he was a fine fellow. He saw himself even with those ideals which he had considered as far beyond him.
quotations.context: Immediately after surviving the first charge, and minutes before the second.
quotations.analysis: The verbs are all of perception — felt, saw — because nothing has been established except a sensation. Crane places this self-congratulation directly before the flight so that the reader watches an identity get assembled and demolished inside a single short chapter.

quotations.text: To the youth it was an onslaught of redoubtable dragons.
quotations.context: As the second attack comes on and the men around him begin to break.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'to the youth' is the hinge: Crane marks the image as Henry's own, so the dragons are a boy's reading matter arriving on a battlefield. He will use the same creatures later to congratulate himself on having met them, which is how the novel measures what he has learned.

quotations.text: He had fled, he told himself, because annihilation approached.
quotations.context: Alone in the woods, constructing a defence of his flight.
quotations.analysis: 'He told himself' is the whole technique in three words: the sentence reports a proposition without adopting it. The Latinate 'annihilation' is several registers above anything Henry says out loud, which marks the reasoning as a performance for an audience of one.

quotations.text: There was the law, he said. Nature had given him a sign.
quotations.context: After throwing a pine cone at a squirrel, which runs away.
quotations.analysis: He has conducted an experiment designed to produce the result he wanted and calls the result a law. Crane lets the reasoning stand for a page and then walks him into a dead man's face, which is nature's other sign and is not addressed to him at all.

quotations.text: It was the religion of peace. It would die if its timid eyes were compelled to see blood. He conceived Nature to be a woman with a deep aversion to tragedy.
quotations.context: Walking deeper into the woods, away from the sound of the guns.
quotations.analysis: 'He conceived' marks the whole proposition as Henry's invention, and the gendering of Nature as a squeamish woman is the sentimental nineteenth-century picture the book exists to dismantle. Three sentences later he pushes aside the green boughs and finds the corpse.

quotations.text: The corpse was dressed in a uniform that had once been blue, but was now faded to a melancholy shade of green.
quotations.context: In the clearing of pine boughs that Henry has just described as a chapel.
quotations.analysis: A Union uniform has decayed into the colour of the forest, so the man has been absorbed by the landscape rather than commemorated by it. Crane spends the rest of the paragraph on ants moving across the face: the detail is clinical, and the only emotion in the sentence has been transferred onto a colour.

quotations.text: Where yeh hit, ol’ boy?
quotations.speaker: The tattered soldier
quotations.context: In the column of wounded men, asked in what Crane calls a brotherly tone.
quotations.analysis: It is the friendliest sentence in the novel and the one Henry cannot bear, because among these men the wound is the credential and he has none. The question is asked twice more in the next chapters, and it is what finally drives him to leave a badly hurt man alone in a field.

quotations.text: He wished that he, too, had a wound, a red badge of courage.
quotations.context: Walking among men whose injuries he has begun to envy.
quotations.analysis: The title phrase appears once, in Henry's mind, as a wish — which makes the whole book the story of a metaphor he goes looking for and then receives by accident. A badge is worn to be read by others, so what he wants is not courage but the sign of it.

quotations.text: The red sun was pasted in the sky like a wafer.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the chapter, immediately after Jim Conklin's death.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is flat, domestic and slightly absurd, and it stands alone as a paragraph where a novel of 1895 would normally place a reflection. Whether the wafer is a communion host or a seal on an envelope has been argued for a century; either way the sky is doing nothing, and the refusal to say more is the point.

quotations.text: He felt that he was regarding a procession of chosen beings.
quotations.context: Watching a column of troops move up towards the fighting.
quotations.analysis: Men marching into danger become a religious procession because he is looking at them from outside, and the novel is careful that this is a matter of position rather than of merit. A few pages later he privately hopes the army will be beaten, so that his flight will look like foresight.

quotations.text: He adroitly and fiercely swung his rifle. It crushed upon the youth’s head. The man ran on.
quotations.context: In a retreating crowd, after Henry grabs at a man to ask what has happened.
quotations.analysis: Three short sentences, no adjective of feeling, and the assailant is gone before the second one ends. This is the wound the regiment will read as evidence of courage, delivered by a panicking Union soldier to a man who has run away — the novel's central irony arrives in nineteen words and is never commented on.

quotations.text: He had been out among the dragons, he said, and he assured himself that they were not so hideous as he had imagined them.
quotations.context: The morning after his return to the regiment, with his head bandaged.
quotations.analysis: Two verbs of self-address in one sentence — he said, he assured himself — and the dragons are the same ones he ran from in Chapter VI. The revision is complete: an experience he did not have is now a qualification, and the reader is shown the machinery rather than told about it.

quotations.text: It was not well to drive men into final corners; at those moments they could all develop teeth and claws.
quotations.context: Henry's state of mind before the fighting in which the regiment is told to hold.
quotations.analysis: The proposition is offered as general wisdom and is in fact a threat made by a frightened man to nobody in particular. Crane has been describing armies as animals since Chapter II, and here the imagery finally arrives inside Henry's own account of himself.

quotations.text: they now looked upon him as a war devil.
quotations.context: After Henry keeps firing at an enemy that has already withdrawn.
quotations.analysis: The reputation is made by men watching him rather than by anything he decided, and the thing they watched was him failing to notice that the fighting had stopped. Courage in this novel is consistently a reading made by other people of behaviour that had some quite different cause.

quotations.text: They fight like a lot ’a mule drivers. I can spare them best of any.
quotations.speaker: An officer
quotations.context: Two officers on horseback, discussing which regiment to send in, within hearing of Henry and Wilson.
quotations.analysis: The regiment's finest hour is arranged in a sentence about expendability, and the two men who overhear it go back and say nothing. Everything Henry does in the last six chapters is fuelled by an insult, which means the novel's climax of courage has an entirely petty engine.

quotations.text: It was a woman, red and white, hating and loving, that called him with the voice of his hopes.
quotations.context: As Henry takes the regimental colours from a dying sergeant.
quotations.analysis: The flag is given the only romantic attachment in the novel, and it is granted invulnerability precisely because Henry needs something in the field that cannot be killed. Note that the colours are described by their colours: the book's whole palette turns up in one object a man can carry.

quotations.text: He found that he could look back upon the brass and bombast of his earlier gospels and see them truly.
quotations.context: Marching away from the field in the rain, reviewing everything that has happened.
quotations.analysis: He congratulates himself on having seen through his own self-congratulation, which is the same operation one level up. The novel's difficulty is concentrated here: nothing in the sentence is false, and nothing in it is evidence, since the man assessing the account is the man who wrote it.

quotations.text: He had been to touch the great death, and found that, after all, it was but the great death. He was a man.
quotations.context: The settled conclusion of his review of himself.
quotations.analysis: The repetition of 'the great death' drains the phrase between its first appearance and its second, which is either maturity or the deflation of a boy's word. Then four monosyllables award him the title he wanted in Chapter I, and the book declines to say whether the award is deserved.

quotations.text: Over the river a golden ray of sun came through the hosts of leaden rain clouds.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: It is the shape of a consoling ending without the content of one: a ray of sun, a river, and no statement about what any of it means. 'Hosts' is the only word carrying any military weight, and it belongs to the clouds — the weather keeps the vocabulary of armies, and the armies have marched off the page.

timeline.label: The American Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The war Crane's novel is set in, and which he was born too late to see.

timeline.label: The Battle of Chancellorsville
timeline.detail: Fought in Virginia in early May: confused fighting in woodland, and a Union defeat. Long associated with the novel, though Crane never names it.

timeline.label: The war ends
timeline.detail: Veterans' reminiscences, many of them published in magazines Crane read, became a large part of American periodical writing.

timeline.label: Stephen Crane born in Newark, New Jersey
timeline.detail: The fourteenth child of a Methodist minister, and six years too late for the war he made his name on.

timeline.label: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets
timeline.detail: Crane's first novel, printed at his own expense and largely unsold.

timeline.label: A shortened version syndicated in newspapers
timeline.detail: The story reached its first readers cut down for the press, before any publisher would take the full book.

timeline.label: Published by D. Appleton and Company
timeline.detail: The book made Crane famous in his early twenties, in Britain as well as in America.

timeline.label: Shipwrecked off the Florida coast
timeline.detail: The sinking of the Commodore, on a gun-running voyage to Cuba, produced 'The Open Boat'.

timeline.label: War correspondent in Cuba
timeline.detail: Reporting the Spanish-American War finally gave him the experience readers had assumed lay behind the novel.

timeline.label: Crane dies at Badenweiler
timeline.detail: Of tuberculosis, in a German sanatorium, aged twenty-eight.

timeline.label: John Huston's film
timeline.detail: With Audie Murphy, one of the most decorated American soldiers of the Second World War, as Henry; the studio cut it heavily before release.

places.name: Chancellorsville, Virginia
places.note: The battle of May 1863 most often matched to the novel's circumstances, though the text names nothing.

places.name: Fredericksburg, Virginia
places.note: The town on the Rappahannock beside which the armies of the novel's sort of campaign were camped through the winter.

places.name: New York
places.note: Where D. Appleton and Company published the book in 1895, and where Crane had been living as a struggling reporter.

places.name: Badenweiler, Germany
places.note: The spa town where Crane died of tuberculosis in 1900, five years after the novel appeared.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest account of Crane's method treats the book as painting rather than reporting: colour before information, fragments of sensation, a battlefield assembled from what one pair of eyes can register in smoke.
criticalViews.counter: Read only as technique, the book's moral argument disappears — and the argument about self-deception is conducted in sentences, not in colours.

criticalViews.summary: On this reading Henry is a specimen: an organism acted on by crowd, terrain and instinct, in a universe with nothing to say about him, and courage is simply what the machinery produces under certain loads.
criticalViews.counter: The book keeps giving Henry choices he is capable of assessing — the tattered soldier is the clearest — and it is hard to convict a man of nothing while the novel is so plainly convicting him.

criticalViews.summary: The last chapter can be read as genuine maturity or as the final and most sophisticated act of self-justification in the book; a century of criticism has divided on the question, and the text supports both readings without settling either.
criticalViews.counter: The strongest evidence against simple growth is the tattered man, whose memory Henry has to push away in the same paragraphs where he declares himself free of shame.

criticalViews.summary: The 1895 Appleton book is shorter than Crane's manuscript, and editions built from the manuscript restore passages of Henry's reasoning and alter the weight of the ending. The question of which text to read is therefore also a question about how ironic the book is.
criticalViews.counter: The Appleton text is the one that was read for a century and made the novel's reputation, which is an argument for treating it as the book rather than as a mutilation of one.

essayQuestions.question: How does Crane use point of view to make the reader distrust Henry Fleming?
plan: Establish the technique: third-person narration that borrows Henry's diction, with markers such as 'he told himself' and 'he conceived'.
Work through the squirrel episode in Chapter VII, where an experiment is designed to produce its own conclusion.
Contrast the inflated vocabulary of Henry's self-defence with the flat reporting of the rifle blow in Chapter XII.
Consider how the reader is denied any information Henry lacks, and what that costs and gains.
Apply the whole method to Chapter XXIV, and decide whether the final assessment can be trusted.

essayQuestions.question: 'The wound is the novel's central irony.' Discuss.
plan: Set out what Henry wants in Chapter IX: not courage but a visible mark that certifies it.
Describe how the wound is actually received, and from whom.
Trace the regiment's misreading and Wilson's care in Chapters XIII–XIV.
Weigh the later fighting: does a false credential make the subsequent bravery false?
Conclude on what the book suggests about all reputations, including the ones it calls deserved.

essayQuestions.question: What part does nature play in the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Landscape, indifference and the refusal of meaning
plan: Begin with the opening sentence, where the weather acts and the army is acted on.
Set the squirrel and the 'religion of peace' against the corpse in the pine chapel.
Analyse the wafer simile as a refusal of the consolation the moment calls for.
Note where nature is described as female or sympathetic, and whose language that is.
Close on the last sentence, and whether its golden ray means anything at all.

essayQuestions.question: How far is courage in this novel a property of individuals?
essayQuestions.focus: The regiment, the crowd and the insult
plan: Use Chapter III's moving box and Chapter V's common personality to show courage arriving collectively.
Show the flight in Chapter VI beginning with other men's movement rather than with a decision.
Examine the mule-driver conversation as the actual cause of the final charges.
Consider Wilson, who changes quietly and never narrates it, as a control on Henry.
Decide what is left of individual courage once the crowd, the insult and the accident are subtracted.

discussionQuestions: Crane never names the battle, the cause or the year. What does the novel gain by withholding all of it?
Henry is 'the youth' for most of the book. What changes when a character is described rather than named?
The tattered soldier is the only thing the last chapter cannot absorb. Why does Crane leave him there?
Wilson changes without ever explaining himself to anyone. Is he the novel's answer to Henry, or simply a quieter version of him?
Crane had never seen a battle when he wrote this. Does that matter to what the book is doing?

related.why: The other great American naturalist short novel: instinct, environment and a creature reshaped by pressure rather than by decision.
A comparable New England compression — few characters, a short span, and a landscape that refuses to comfort anybody.
American prose on a vastly larger scale, and the earlier version of the question about how much a man can know of what he is inside.
The novel that put the argument behind this war in front of a mass readership, forty years before Crane's private stopped caring why he was fighting.
Another American book built entirely out of one young narrator's limited view, published a decade earlier.
